chunks: "A diode is a PN junction: a piece of silicon doped P-type on one side and N-type on the other.
When you first form the junction, electrons from the N side diffuse into the P side and holes diffuse the other way, and they recombine.
That leaves a thin region near the junction with no free carriers, just fixed ions: negative on the P side, positive on the N side.
Those ions set up an electric field and a built-in potential barrier, and at equilibrium the field's drift exactly cancels the diffusion.
If I forward bias it, positive on the P side, I'm lowering that barrier.
The number of carriers energetic enough to get over it goes up exponentially, so the current goes up by about ten times for every 60 millivolts.
That's why a silicon diode looks like it 'turns on' at roughly 0. 6 to 0. 7 volts. If I reverse bias it, I make the barrier taller and the depletion region wider.
Now majority carriers can't cross, and the only current is a tiny leakage from minority carriers, nanoamps for a small-signal diode.
Push the reverse voltage far enough and the field gets strong enough to cause avalanche or Zener breakdown.
So the one-line summary is: it conducts easily one way and blocks the other, and the forward current follows the Shockley equation, I equals I S(e to the V over nV T minus 1) ."
